Please read /papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/research-progress/handoffs/10_NATURAL_HAMILTONIAN_BRAINSTORM_CONTINUATION_20261103.md. I want to brainstorm about the form of a natural Hamiltonian, as the note says. First I'd like to draw attention to the formulas for f_i, g_j, their overlap determining the coefficients c, and the multiparticle overlap determining the desired determinant. I think by redefining some of these wavefunctions we might be able to write that as a Hamiltonian expectation value. Can you write down those equations and consider ways that this could be written as an energy expectation value. I am specifically thinking that the theta primitive could be related to the density matrix in equilibrium, possibly using the thermofield double formalism. Please see equation 2.3 from this paper that I published on arxiv in 2020 [https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02713](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02713) to see the type of equation that I'm talking about. 

Please write any research notes from this discussion within the brainstorm folder within 01_mellin_curvature. I might want to start a new investigation for this, because I think the open quantum dynamics folder is too closely tied to previous ideas, and it might be good to start fresh. Please also save the chat history within 01_mellin_curvature/chat-histories.

I’ll read the handoff and your paper, recover the overlap formulas, and work through possible equilibrium and thermofield-double interpretations. I’ll save any notes in the Mellin-curvature brainstorm folder and the chat history in its chat-histories folder.

The handoff gives exactly the mixed overlaps you have in mind. Equation 2.3 in your paper suggests a useful next step: represent the theta heat trace by a thermofield state, then carry the source’s polynomial energy factor into that state. I’m checking which changes preserve the signed determinant and which produce only its squared magnitude.

I’m using the PDF skill to check the notation in your equation directly. The key distinction so far is that the primitive is a partition function with an \(e^u\) prefactor, while \(\Phi\) includes the energy factor \(P_0(\beta H)=2(\beta H)^2-3\beta H\). Both have exact thermofield representations, but their normalized states differ.

There is a useful redefinition: replace the averaged energy response in \(f_i\) by the corresponding energy-dependent operator acting on a filtered thermofield state. Pairing it with the lifted \(g_j\) preserves every coefficient and determinant exactly, although the \(f_i\) norms change.

I also found a narrow constraint: a single self-adjoint operator cannot map every \(g_i\) to the original \(f_i\) with the same labels, because their cross-overlap matrix is not symmetric. The thermofield construction gives us a way to explore beyond that particular assignment.

The thermofield route now gives an explicit formula for the signed determinant as one expectation value. The observable is a many-copy expression built from the energy responses and moment functions; it is not simply the sum of the particle energies. That leaves a concrete next question: whether one natural interaction or response principle generates these expressions across orders. I’m saving the derivation, including the changed norms and that remaining distinction.
